problem.title: On-device visual inspection
problem.context: A manufacturer inspects parts for defects with cameras along its production lines. There are 40 lines in three plants, each with two to four cameras attached to a small edge computer. The plants' network is unreliable: some lines are cut off for days at a time. Quality inspectors label images of defects, about 5,000 new labels a week, and the model is retrained every week from them and pushed to the devices. The team is two ML engineers and one person who spends half their time on operations. The infrastructure budget is tight.

requirements.text: Check every part as it passes the camera and signal a defective part to the line operator.
Retrain the model every week from the newly labelled images and roll the new model out to every line.
Collect the images the model was unsure about, or got wrong, so that inspectors can label them.
Each image is classified on the line within 200 ms, so the line never slows down.
When a plant's network is down for up to seven days, its lines keep inspecting with the model they have; the images collected in the meantime are uploaded when the network returns.
A new model reaches every connected line within 24 hours of approval. When a new model misbehaves on a line, the line operator can go back to the previous one within 15 minutes, without the ML team.
Cloud and infrastructure spending stays under 2,000 euros a month.
Three people build and run the system, with no support outside working hours.
The edge computers (an ARM processor with a small neural accelerator) cannot be replaced this year.

approaches.idea: What if local inference and a direct cloud fleet control plane keep the system simple?
What if each plant gateway absorbs intermittent connectivity and coordinates local releases?
What if the cloud handles inference as well as training?
approaches.dropped_because: Line decisions depend on network round trips, so the approach cannot reliably meet the 200 ms line latency or keep inspecting through a week-long outage.

approaches.idea: What if a small team keeps direct device delivery but uses human approval at each rollout stage to contain release risk?

values: Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model
trajectory.hypothesis: Local inference and queued images should meet R1, R3, Q1 and Q2; central training and direct OTA should support R2 and Q3 with low operating overhead for C1 and Q4.
trajectory.observation: Offline inspection and collection are natural at the edge. Direct fleet delivery can reach connected lines, but safe rollout and the limited operations capacity need clearer safeguards.

values: Model distribution: Gateway relay to lines
Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model
trajectory.hypothesis: Keeping inference on each line meets R1 and Q1; gateway buffering supports Q2 and R3 while relaying models supports R2 and Q3, though gateway operations may pressure Q4 and C1.
trajectory.observation: The gateway gives plants a natural transfer boundary, but a plant-by-plant rollout alone does not guarantee safe canarying or fast operator rollback.

trajectory.hypothesis: Central inference and retention simplify R2 and R3, but dependence on the plant network is likely to fail R1, Q1 and Q2.
trajectory.observation: Network round trips undermine the stated latency and outages halt inspection. Those are stressed requirements that no cloud-side adjustment can fix while inference remains remote.

values: Rollout policy: Canary with health-gated expansion
Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model
trajectory.hypothesis: Changing rollout to health-gated canary expansion should improve Q3 without adding a plant service, preserving Q4 and C1 while retaining local rollback.
trajectory.observation: A health-gated canary addresses propagation risk while preserving rollback at the line. Automated release handling keeps operational work within the small team, with storage sizing still to be specified.

values: Model distribution: Gateway relay to lines
Rollout policy: Canary within each plant
Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model
trajectory.hypothesis: Per-plant canaries and local relaying should improve Q3 and Q2, but additional gateway costs and care may burden Q4 and C1.
trajectory.observation: Plant-local staging isolates network outages and limits rollout blast radius. The additional gateway fleet consumes budget and creates another component for the small team.

values: Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model
trajectory.hypothesis: Human approval between rollout stages may make direct delivery easier to supervise for C1 and Q3, while a gateway preserves collected images across outages; added hardware and approval work may pressure Q4 and C1.
trajectory.observation: Approval adds control but creates operator work and can delay reaching every connected line within 24 hours. Gateway buffering improves outage collection at an infrastructure cost, so this is a cautious but complex fallback.

values: Rollout policy: Canary with health-gated expansion
Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model
Queue capacity: Seven-day edge image buffer
trajectory.hypothesis: Reserving edge storage for the full seven-day outage scenario should strengthen Q2 and R3 while retaining health-gated rollout, local rollback and low infrastructure cost.
trajectory.observation: Explicit capacity planning makes the offline collection promise credible, though local disk limits and retention policy need operations attention. Automated fleet handling keeps operational work within the staffing constraint.

values: Model distribution: Gateway relay to lines
Rollout policy: Canary within each plant
Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model
Queue capacity: Seven-day plant gateway image buffer
trajectory.hypothesis: Reserving a full outage week of gateway storage should strengthen Q2 and R3 while protecting the local canary design, with additional cost and maintenance burden.
trajectory.observation: Gateway capacity provides a clear outage buffer target but reinforces the capital and operational cost that distinguishes this design.

values: Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model
Approval window: Each stage approved within four working hours
trajectory.hypothesis: A defined approval window should make human-gated rollout more predictable for Q3, though availability of the part-time operator remains a constraint for C1.
trajectory.observation: A working-hours target bounds approval delay but cannot guarantee expansion within 24 hours when approvals span nights or weekends. Gateway buffering improves outage collection, but this remains a cautious and operationally weaker option.

alternatives.summary: Run inference and image buffering on the existing line computers, then send weekly models directly from a central fleet service with canary health gates and local operator rollback.

choices.reason: Local classification meets the line latency and outage cases on the hardware already installed.
One shared training pipeline supports weekly retraining without plant-specific ML operations.
Uncertain or incorrect images can be retained locally and uploaded after connectivity returns.
Direct rollout avoids a separate gateway fleet and can reach connected devices promptly.

adrs.title: Where should part classification run?
adrs.context: The line must signal defects within 200 ms and continue through a seven-day plant network outage. The existing ARM edge computers cannot be replaced this year, so inference must fit their available accelerator capacity.

options.name: Local edge inference
pros: Avoids network round trips on every part.
cons: The model must fit and be optimized for the installed edge hardware.
options.reason: All retained alternatives meet the line latency and outage needs by running inference locally.

options.name: Central cloud inference
pros: Centralizes model serving and simplifies per-device inference deployment.
cons: Network delay and disconnection prevent timely or continuous line decisions.
options.reason: It misses the most constraining latency and availability scenarios.

adrs.title: How should weekly learning and image collection work?
adrs.context: Inspectors label about 5,000 images weekly, and the model is retrained weekly. Images selected for review must survive network outages, while the small team needs one manageable training process.

options.name: Central training with edge queues
values: Queue capacity: Seven-day edge image buffer
pros: One training workflow can consume the collected labels weekly.
Each line can retain images for the full outage period until upload resumes.
cons: Edge storage needs capacity limits and upload retry handling.
options.reason: This keeps collection resilient while avoiding another plant-side training system.

options.name: Central training with plant relays
values: Queue capacity: Seven-day plant gateway image buffer
pros: Plant relays can aggregate uploads across lines and forward after outages.
cons: Gateways add hardware and a component to maintain.
options.reason: This alternative prefers plant-level transfer buffering for lines sharing an unreliable uplink.

options.name: Central training with plant relays and human gates
pros: One training workflow pairs with plant-level buffering for disconnected lines.
cons: Gateway hardware adds infrastructure cost alongside the human approval workload.
options.reason: This combination joins outage-resilient collection with deliberate release oversight.

adrs.title: How should approved models reach lines and recover from a bad release?
adrs.context: Every connected line must receive a weekly model within 24 hours, and an operator must restore the prior version within 15 minutes without ML staff. Rollout and recovery must fit a small operations team and the infrastructure budget.

options.name: Direct canary rollout
values: Rollout policy: Canary with health-gated expansion

pros: Few infrastructure components and automated expansion after health checks.
Local rollback supports a line operator.
cons: Device fleet connectivity and health signals must be managed reliably.
options.reason: It combines prompt direct delivery with safeguards while limiting infrastructure cost.

cons: Gateway purchase, monitoring and maintenance consume budget and team time.
options.reason: This is appropriate when local transfer control is worth the extra plant infrastructure.

options.name: Human-approved direct rollout
values: Rollback control: Operator selects previous local model

pros: Explicit human review can catch problems before rollout expansion.
Direct delivery keeps infrastructure needs low.
cons: Approval availability can delay the 24-hour target and adds operations work.
options.reason: This favors deliberate oversight where release risk outweighs rollout speed.

options.name: Unstaged central service release
pros: A central service has one release point.
cons: It depends on network access and leaves line operators unable to roll back locally.
options.reason: It cannot meet outage availability or the operator-led local rollback scenario.
